opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underappreciated points in the whole debate. There's a line of argument that goes: if you take a base model and sample from it a thousand times, pass@1000, it'll eventually get the right answer, so RL isn't teaching it anything new, it's just sharpening a distribution that was already there. I think that framing is technically true in a narrow sense but misses what actually matters.

Think about what "given enough tries" means in practice. If the correct answer is somewhere in a thousand samples, you still need a way to pick it out, and for most real-world tasks you don't have a perfect verifier sitting there. And for agentic, multi-step tasks it compounds badly. If each step has a few plausible branches and only one leads anywhere useful, the probability of stumbling down the right path across fifty or a hundred steps by chance is effectively zero. So narrowing the model toward meaningful actions isn't a cosmetic improvement, it's the difference between a capability that exists in principle and one you can actually use.

There's also a nice analogy to people. A smart undergrad might, in some sense, contain the ability to write a great research paper. Most of what a PhD does is teach taste: which directions to pursue, which to drop, how to not waste six months on a dead end. You're not giving them a fundamentally new brain, you're shaping where they spend their effort. That shaping is enormously valuable, and I'd argue it's a big part of what expertise is.

And I'd push back a little on the idea that RL only reweights what's there. Once the model reliably takes good actions, it reaches states it would almost never reach otherwise, gets feedback there, and learns from that. So the narrowing bootstraps into genuinely new behavior. Early on it looks like sharpening; over enough training, it looks like learning.

So my assessment is that it's very valuable, and the "the base model could already do it" critique tells us more about how we measure capability than about RL's limits. The real question is whether RL can keep extending the frontier on long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards, and from what we've seen so far, I'm fairly optimistic.

r001.rationale: The response says that narrowing toward meaningful actions makes success practical on long, multi-step tasks, where random branching is unlikely to work, and describes the model as reliably taking good actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually a really underrated point. People sometimes look at the pass-at-k results, where the base model gets the right answer in one of a hundred or one of a thousand samples, and conclude that RL isn't teaching the model anything new, it's just sharpening a distribution. And in a narrow sense that's true. But I think that framing undersells what's happening.

Think about it from the perspective of actually using the model. If I'm an agent trying to accomplish something in the world, I don't get a thousand tries. I get one, maybe a handful. So the difference between "the correct action is somewhere in the model's support" and "the correct action is the thing the model actually does" is enormous. That's the whole ballgame for whether the model is useful. A base model is a bit like a very well-read person who has no idea which of their thoughts are worth acting on. RL is what gives it taste, or judgment, about which path to take.

And I'd push back a little on the idea that it's purely narrowing. When you do RL over long horizons, you're not just reweighting individual answers. You're shaping the model's policy over sequences of actions, including things like when to backtrack, when to check its work, when to ask for more information. Those behaviors can be composed of pieces that were all latent in the base model, sure, but the composition itself was never going to be sampled reliably. The probability mass on the full correct trajectory might be astronomically small before RL, even if each step is individually plausible.

There's also a version of this from the interpretability side that I find interesting. When you look at what changes in the model during RL, it often isn't that brand new circuits appear. It's that existing features get routed differently, the model learns to attend to the right things at the right moments. That's consistent with the "narrowing" story, but it also means the narrowing is happening at the level of internal computation, not just the output distribution. So it's less like filtering a list of answers and more like learning which internal processes to trust.

Where I think the skeptics have a real point is on generalization. If RL is mostly sharpening, then you might worry it's sharpening toward the specific distribution of your reward environments, and the model will be brittle outside of them. That's an empirical question, and I think the honest answer is that it varies. But even in the pessimistic case, going from a thousand tries to one try on the tasks people actually care about is a lot of value. I wouldn't dismiss it just because the base model "technically" could have done it.

r001.rationale: The response says RL makes the correct action what the model actually does on one or a few tries, describing that as essential to usefulness and contrasting it with merely having the answer somewhere in the base model’s support.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a lot of the value of reinforcement learning. There’s a huge difference between a model that can produce the right answer once in a thousand tries and one that reliably produces it on the first try. Even if you haven’t expanded what’s possible for the model to generate, you’ve made that capability much more useful.

And that becomes especially important when you’re taking a sequence of actions. If you have to make lots of correct decisions in a row, you can’t afford to sample a thousand times at every step. You might not even have a way to recognize which action was correct until much later.

So I wouldn’t dismiss narrowing the distribution as merely eliciting something that was already there. Learning which of the things you could do are actually worth doing is a substantial part of intelligence. The interesting question is how well that learning generalizes—whether you’re getting better at selecting useful actions in new situations, or just getting more reliable on the situations you trained on.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning makes a correct answer reliable on the first try instead of rare, describing that as a key value of narrowing the distribution toward useful actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s hugely valuable. There’s a big difference between a model that can produce the right answer somewhere in a million samples and a model that reliably produces it on the first try. The first tells you that the capability is in there, in some sense. But you still have to find it, and recognizing the right answer might itself be difficult.

Reinforcement learning can change where the model spends its probability mass. It can take this enormous space of possible responses and concentrate it on actions that actually make progress. And when you’re doing a sequence of actions, that matters enormously. If you keep taking slightly unhelpful steps, you’re unlikely to end up accomplishing a difficult task.

So even if you haven’t expanded what the model could conceivably generate, you may have dramatically expanded what it can practically accomplish. I wouldn’t dismiss that as just eliciting something that was already there. Making a capability reliable and affordable is a substantial part of making it useful.

r001.rationale: It explains that reinforcement learning concentrates probability on actions that make progress, making the model reliably produce useful outputs and practically accomplish difficult tasks.
